newsitem.title: ITALY: Star magistrate's election bid divides Italy.
newsitem.headline: Star magistrate's election bid divides Italy.

text.p: Former star anti-graft magistrate Antonio Di Pietro's decision to run for parliament on a centre-left ticket has divided the Italian political world and exposed cracks in Prime Minister Romano Prodi's coalition.
Di Pietro, a former public works minister in the Prodi government, announced on Wednesday night he would run for a Senate seat in a Tuscan district about to become vacant.
But the decision by the magistrate, who became a folk hero because of his Milan-based Mani Pulite (Clean Hands) probes of corruption in the early 1990s, caused a summer political storm.
Di Pietro was convinced to seek the seat by Massimo D'Alema, head of the Democratic Party of the Left (PDS), largest party in Prodi's centre-left "Olive Treee" coalition.

Di Pietro, who left the magistrature in December 1994 for reasons that have never fully been explained, is currently under investigation by magistrates in the city of Brescia on suspicion of alleged irregularities while he was a magistrate.

The Brescia magistrates had already cleared Di Pietro of several accusations of corruption. They are currently probing allegations that his wife, a lawyer, received gifts and loans from a leading Italian constructor.
The constructor, Antonio d'Adamo, was in turn linked to a Swiss-Italian banker Milan magistrates had investigated for corruption.

Former Prime Minister Silvio Berlusconi, himself the subject of probes by Milan magistrates, accused Di Pietro of seeking the seat in an attempt to protect himself from the possibility of prosecution in the future.
"The mask is off ... a strange magistrate with a habit of running up debts has decided to seek parliamentary immunity. I wish him luck," Berlusconi said.
Although Italian parliamentarians no longer enjoy immunity from investigation they still enjoy some privileges if probed.
A number of supporters of Prodi's coalition, however, said they were against the move.

"You can't offer a parliamentary seat and the immunity that derives from it to a person who has just been been caught up in a judicial storm," said Mauro Paissan, head of the Greens in the lower house of parliament.

"There was no need for this ... this was a senseless decision. This is madness," said Fausto Bertinotti, whose hard-left Communist Refoundation party shores up Prodi's majority in the Chamber of Deputies (lower house).
Di Pietro said he was not seeking parliamentary privileges.

"Parliamentary immunity does not exist any more. Don't these people in (Rome) know that?" Di Pietro was quoted as saying by the Rome newspaper La Repubblica, adding that by the time the election was held, the investigation underway in Brescia would have run its course.
Under a 1993 law magistrates no longer have to ask parliament to probe MPs but they still must seek permission to arrest a member, tap a telephone or search a home or office.
Di Pietro said a number of parliamentarians of Berlusconi's Forza Italia party had their own judicial problems and held office just the same.

The former magistrate, one of Italy's best-known figures, said he had decided to run for the seat because he wanted to help strengthen what he called the "moderate" part of the centre-left coalition backing Prodi.
Di Pietro resigned as public works minister in the Prodi government after six months in 1996 when he came under investigation by the Brescia magistrates.
He said at the time that he had become the victim of a "pigeon shoot" and could not do his job in those circumstances.
